content.thinking:
There's already a soulScythe.ts sample file, but I'll ignore it and write fresh rather than risk copying inconsistent patterns—I'll just be careful to typecheck afterward. For the design, I'm thinking a dragonbone soul scythe in a League of Legends style, ornate and hand-painted like a Thresh-inspired soul-fighter weapon.

I'm deciding the orientation convention: model faces +Z means the blade's flat face should point toward the viewer, so the scythe stands upright with the blade sweeping sideways toward +X. For the shaft, I'm planning a 2-meter snath with the butt at y=0 and top around 1.9, slightly curved using a smooth spline.

For the shaft itself, I'm building it as a dragon spine: a thin glowing teal core rod surrounded by roughly 22 bone-colored vertebrae disks with small lateral spikes, spaced along the sweep with visible glowing gaps between segments to suggest soul energy flowing through. At the base, I'm capping it with a gold-and-bone dragon talon foot with three claw prongs touching the ground.

For the grip, I want leather wraps with cloth strips and gold rings, plus a hanging chain detail — similar to Thresh's lantern scythe — with a small soul lantern dangling near the top of the shaft, swinging from a short chain around y=1.45 down to about y=1.15-1.3.

I'm hanging the lantern from a curved bone hook on the opposite side of the shaft from the blade, so the weapon stays visually balanced, positioning it at x=-0.17. For the head assembly, I'm envisioning a dragon skull capping the shaft at the top, with the blade emerging as a massive curved rib-bone or horn carved from ivory bone and lit with a glowing teal soul-edge, the skull itself featuring a glowing eye facing outward.

The skull jaws bite the blade root where it emerges, and the blade itself curves out horizontally from there before dropping into a scythe-like point, with a concave cutting edge below and a spined outer edge above, plus small bone-spike serrations along the spine and a thin glowing teal soul-edge extrude along the inner blade for extra detail; I'm also adding a smaller secondary backspike horn on the opposite side as a counter-curve.

Mapping out the precise blade profile coordinates now to get the curve of the outer spine and the concave inner cutting edge right, with the tip curling sharply downward.

Still working out the claw tip coordinates...

I'll use smoothing with sharp corners for the tip while testing with a preview to ensure the cuts don't overlap, then move to the blade's bone-ivory gradient paint layer with painted cracks.

For the edge glow, I'm computing a teal shimmer based on distance from the blade's inner edge, then building a separate emissive strip geometry offset slightly above that inner edge to simulate a glowing soul-steel seam... Building edge strip geometry...

Simpler: make the bone body the full blade extrude with a bevel, then add a slightly thicker glowing edge strip flush along the rim on both faces for that teal glow look. I also want to add rune textures on the blade faces using decal planes with glowing SVG markings, placed front and back along the blade's curve.

Now I'm thinking through additional details like a dark fuller groove running from root to tip, thin rib bones radiating like dragon claws, and spine serrations as spikes positioned along the top-edge curve using a catmull path.

Now I'm defining the model-space orientation for the outline, with x and y axes forming the face plane and z as thickness, then sketching the dragon skull head dimensions and how it sits atop the shaft with the blade root offset to one side.

Thinking through the composition: skull faces +Z toward the viewer while the blade emerges from the back of the cranium and sweeps outward along +X, placing the blade's plane at a slight negative z offset so it reads behind the skull in a front view.

For the skull itself, I'm planning a part-based build from the shaft's top: a cervical neck cap, a cranium from a scaled sphere, a forward snout frustum, an upper jaw with teeth, and possibly a separate lower jaw. I need to figure out joint structure too -- since parts require a bone, I'm considering a root joint plus additional joints for head, jaw, and lantern, checking how similar weapon samples handle this.

I'm shaping the cranium as a faceted low-poly sphere for a bony look, then working out the snout and jaw geometry using lofted profiles along the skull's length.

I'll build the jaw parts closed first, then pose the jaw bone open with a forward-downward rotation so attached geometry follows naturally. I'll add glowing teal elements for the eye sockets, mouth interior, and a soul-core flame to give it that eerie lit-from-within look, then move on to shaping the backward-swept horns.

Still working out the horn curves, spike ridges, brow geometry, and teeth placement along the jaw, while figuring out where the neck shaft should meet the base of the skull.

Scaling things up: total height around 2.3 meters with the blade root near y=1.9, spanning from a top tip of 2.18 down to a lower tip around 1.48, giving it a grand stylized scythe proportion. Now working out the shaft curve from the butt at y=0.02 up to y=1.85, using a slight S-shaped catmull-rom path with small z offsets to give it a natural bend.

I'm figuring out how to place vertebrae segments along this curved shaft path using frame-based positioning, where each segment's lathe geometry gets aligned so its local axis follows the tangent of the curve, with an embed value of zero centering each piece at its frame point.

Now I'm sketching the vertebra shape itself as an hourglass-profile lathe geometry built from a small set of radius points, plus deciding where the dorsal spine spikes and transverse processes should project relative to the spine's curve.

I'm settling on three zones along the shaft: a lower vertebrae cluster from 0.18–0.52, the wrapped grip from 0.55–1.0, and a longer vertebrae run from 1.03–1.75. I'm also adding a continuous teal glow rod running the length from 0.1 to 1.8, peeking through the gaps between vertebrae segments.

Now I'm covering the grip area with a leather sweep using a dark brown-purple grain color, then adding a thin spiral strap wrap in teal-trimmed cloth around it using a spiral path helper that takes a center point, start point, axis, and turn/pitch parameters.

Adding gold torus collars at grip ends...

For decoration, I'm hanging 3-4 tattered ribbon tassels in teal/indigo with gold tips from a ring around the shaft near y=1.78, using double-sided card frames sized roughly 0.07 by 0.45. Now I'm thinking about adding a soul lantern hanging from a hook.

Below that, off a secondary shaft near y=1.55 I'm curving a bone horn outward, then dropping 5 small torus chain links of alternating orientation down from the hook tip. The lantern itself is a hexagonal cage with gold lathe caps top and bottom, a glowing teal hex prism as the glass, six thin gold rods as bars, and a flickering soul-flame card glowing inside, sized around 0.12 tall and positioned at y~1.2, offset to x=-0.2 so it clears the shaft, topped with a dragon-claw ring.

I'm skipping a mini skull charm and instead adding 3 small translucent ghost-face card wisps drifting in the concave curve of the blade, each double-sided and glowing with a faint trailing tail -- a nod to the trapped-soul Thresh motif, kept small and few so it doesn't look stray.

Now I'm planning the texture set: blade runes, a soul-wisp ghost texture, an indigo ribbon with gold trim and teal rune, soul-fire for the lantern/mouth glow, and a gold dragon-sigil medallion decal at the collar. For paints, I'm considering a custom ivory bone paint with warm-cool lighting and crack lines tinged teal at the crevices, plus dark bone, leather grain, and a clockwork-style gold metal paint.

I'm deciding to borrow the clockwork kit's gilt metal paint for gold accents while writing my own warm-streaked gold variant for finer control, aiming for a stylized League-of-Legends look with strong value contrast, saturated cyan glow, and gold trim. For the blade paint, I'm computing surface coordinates relative to the blade's origin to drive an ivory-to-green color flow along its length.

Still writing shader logic...

Defining the color palette...

Setting up the Three.js scene with builder and frame imports...

I'm weighing texel density to decide paint resolution — 1024 seems sufficient given the shaft's painted area. Now I'm sketching the skeleton setup, starting with a root joint for the shaft and considering whether to model it as a chain of joints along the shaft's length.

Adding joints for head, jaw, hook, and ribbon...

Still placing more skull features... brows, a tapered snout loft with multiple width/height stations, nostril bumps, and dark eye socket spheres.

I'm working out a snout interpolation function to compute y, width, and height at any z position, which I'll reuse for placing teeth and nostrils, then setting up loft stations for the lower jaw hinge with coordinates at each z depth.

For the open maw I'm planning a hinge rotation of about 22 degrees to drop the jaw tip, plus a glowing teal sphere core and flame texture cards positioned inside the mouth for a soul-flame effect, building the jaw geometry before applying the pose.

Now I'm sketching the horns as tapered bezier curves sweeping back from the cranium on both sides, curling up and back with control points moving from near the skull base outward and downward in z, positioned behind the skull plane on the +X side.

I think it's cleaner to tuck the blade root behind the skull with a socket plate attaching at the cranium's back, pushing the root further back so it embeds directly into the skull geometry rather than crossing the horns. I'll keep the left horn as a free sweep while making the right horn shorter to avoid collision.

For the horn placement, I'm considering having them swing upward and slightly outward above the blade's top edge, though they may poke through the blade plane a bit—which could actually look fine as overlapping, pierced solids. Alternatively, I could curve the horns forward instead, dragon-style, framing the face ahead of the blade's plane entirely to avoid any intersection issue.

Checking cranium position against the blade root — placing blade origin so it emerges from the lower back of the skull like it's attached to the neck, with the horns clearing above. I'm working out the shaft-to-skull junction, with the shaft top ending around y=1.8 tucked beneath the cranium base near y=1.875.

Adding a gold collar at the neck joint with cervical vertebrae pieces angling up to the skull's rear, and checking the jaw hinge and open-mouth geometry don't collide with the collar. The skull feels a bit small relative to the 2.3m weapon scale, so I'm considering bumping it up roughly 30% for a more dramatic, oversized look.

I'm working out a scaling transform applied to the skull's local coordinates relative to its origin point, then re-deriving the collar, shaft, and blade root positions so nothing overlaps once the skull grows.

The blade root will dip slightly behind the cranium at that scale, which seems fine since it's partially hidden anyway. Since I can't fully verify the geometry visually just by reasoning, I'll go ahead and run the preview tool a few times, checking rendered shots and iterating until it looks right.

Now I'm working out the horn placements in skull-local coordinates, sweeping curved horn shapes using path tangent frames rather than normals so the rings and ridges follow the horn's curve correctly. I'm also planning additional skull features — cheek spikes, a three-spike dorsal crest, a small nasal horn, and translucent ear-fin frills with a teal glow — to add more creature detail.

I'm deciding to replace the frill idea with fanned cheek spikes radiating backward from the jaw hinge with graded lengths, and I'm planning a glowing teal gem set into a gold plate on the forehead, seated using surface placement helpers to position it correctly on the cranium's curved surface.

For the crest spikes, I'll scatter them along the back of the cranium at different elevations, oriented along the surface normals so they jut outward naturally. Now I'm also sketching out a gold-plated mounting bracket where the blade root meets the skull, fan-shaped with dragon-scale engraving and thicker extrusion than the surrounding plates.

Adding rivets and spine ribs...

I'm weighing whether to add ribs or rune textures to the blade face, and decide both can coexist: thin bone-colored ribs spanning the upper portion for the dragon-wing look, with a rune glyph strip lower down near the edge for the magical effect.

Writing SVG glyph positions...

I need to figure out the center placement of the rect, then work through how the front and back texture planes should be oriented since the back plane faces -Z and its local u-axis flips direction when rotated 180° about Y, meaning the text orientation as seen from behind needs careful handling so it doesn't appear mirrored incorrectly.

Rather than flipping the whole plane with negative scale, which would break winding and cause culling, the cleaner fix is to flip the UV coordinates on the back plane's geometry so u maps to 1-u, keeping the rune positions aligned with the blade curve while still reading correctly from the back.

I'm applying the same aiming logic for the lantern and setting up the glow on the textured rune planes, keeping colored runes intact. Now I'm working out how the inner edge band polygon should be built from the same inner points, offset back along the blade to form the outline strip.

For the tip, I realize the band width should taper toward zero so it doesn't poke past the blade's rounded corners, so I'm sampling the catmull-spline edges directly to get a smooth silhouette instead of relying on extrude smoothing.

Plotting blade outline key points...

Checking the outline near the tip to make sure the top and inner curves converge properly without crossing, verifying the tip merges to a single sharp point while the root edges stay distinct.

I need to keep the outline under 512 points and define the point type with optional sharp markers. I'll build a lookup function for the inner curve by x-position, then construct an edge band whose width tapers to zero near the tip using a smoothstep function.

Since the top band point at the tip coincides with the last inner point, that duplicate gets dropped automatically. I'm setting the band thickness to 0.04 with a slightly thinner blade value, giving it a teal glow color so the cutting edge visually reads as a thin glowing strip.

Now I'm adding dorsal spines along the blade's back spine at four positions, each oriented outward and angled toward the tip, sized a bit thicker than the blade itself to look like chunky bone barbs resembling dragon spines -- though I think flat curved barb plates would read better than rounded cones.

Working out the curved barb outline...

Defining the gold root clamp polygon...

Now adding the gem stone, teal glow sphere, and gold rivet spheres at four positions. I'm also sketching a secondary dragon motif near the root — a small downward-pointing talon under the blade and a curved bone horn sweeping back from the neck.

I'm tapering that rear horn with vertebra-like ridges and a few small barbs for a swallow-tail silhouette, balancing the overall shape. Thinking I could skip a separate lantern hook entirely and just hang the lantern from the tip of that rear bone spike instead.

Settling on hanging the lantern from the horn tip with a short chain, about 0.28m, so the lantern dangles around y≈1.72 near the left side — creates a nice dramatic asymmetry balanced against the blade on the right.

Building the chain with alternating torus links scaled and rotated to look like a realistic hanging chain, then positioning the lantern body beneath the finial where the chain ends.

Still placing hexagonal bars...

For the base I'm sketching a gold lathe bowl with small downward claw-like spikes, and I'm reconsidering the glow: if the glass body is solid emissive teal, the flame inside won't be visible, so I need to decide whether the glass should be paler and more translucent to let the inner flame card show through.

Writing lantern texture SVG...

Working out card orientation for the flame wisps...

I'm sketching the flame as a teardrop SVG with a teal gradient outer glow and a pale inner core, plus some side tongues for texture. For the ghost-like soul wisps, I'm designing simple spirit figures with trailing tails, dark eyes, and open mouths, placing a few of them tucked beneath the blade's concave curve near the inner edge.

Now I'm figuring out the ribbon details - four cloth ribbons hanging from a gold collar ring near the top of the shaft, indigo fabric with gold trim and teal runes, ending in swallow-tail points, draped around front and back of the collar.

So the drawing appears upside down when hanging: the swallowtail tail end is physically at the top and the attach point at the bottom of the SVG. I'll keep the emblem symmetric, like a diamond with gold stripes, so orientation doesn't matter visually.

For the different ribbons I'll vary their flow direction—front ones facing outward, side ones facing sideways—to show them from multiple angles. For the weapon's butt end, I'm working out the gold ferrule and a bone talon spike pointing down toward the floor, making sure the tip just barely touches or sinks slightly below the ground line.

Actually a better design: three curved dragon-foot talons splaying outward from the ferrule at 120° intervals, acting like tripod legs that let the weapon stand upright on its own, with their claw tips touching the floor at a small radius from center.

Tapering the talon tip to exactly y=0 so the point caps meet cleanly, then moving on to the gold ferrule — faceted lathe scales with a gilt metal finish and slight tarnish for an aged look.

Now I'm defining the color palette: teals and indigos for the main body, golds for metal accents, and a bone paint function for the ribs and dorsal spines, with a darker variant for shading those areas.

Writing bone shader logic...

Now I'm detailing the grip: a leather sleeve with dark plum grain texture, a spiral teal-indigo cloth strap wrapped around it, gold bands capping the ends, and bone knuckle studs between wraps. I'm also considering a mid-shaft gold dragon-scale guard as a secondary grip point.

Now I'm designing lathe-profile collars for the shaft—solid cross-sections flaring from the thin shaft radius out to wider rims near teal gems at two heights, plus a taller flared socket collar near the top mount where the weapon connects to the neck.

I'm adding a ring of six small gold spikes around the neck just below where it meets the cranium/jaw, checking that their position and length won't awkwardly intersect the jaw hinge geometry when open.

Working out the skull placement, I'm positioning the cranium center in skull-space with a small offset and checking that its radius leaves a reasonable gap above the collar, bridging the two with a short neck rod. Now I'm computing the scaled cranium sphere radii for the world-space version.

Mapping out the snout as a series of loft stations with shrinking width and height along the z-axis, then converting those to world coordinates. I'm placing a nose pad sphere, dark nostril spheres, brow ridge rods, and eye sockets with inset glow spheres just inside them.

I'm now checking that eye socket geometry doesn't clash with the cranium's narrowing radius near the snout junction, confirming the sockets sit on the snout's side surface rather than poking through the skull, then starting on the lower jaw's hinge point and loft stations.

I'm working through the lower jaw loft, placing the chin, hinge, and tooth positions, and checking for overlap between the jaw's top surface and the snout's underside before rotating it into the closed position.

Setting the jaw to open 24° around the hinge, defining the jaw bone joint, then laying out upper tooth positions along the snout sides with varying lengths for canines versus incisors.

Still placing teeth geometry... lower teeth mirror the jaw's top surface with longer canines, plus a glowing flame soul placed inside the mouth. Now I'm plotting horn curve control points in skull space, sweeping outward and up on both sides.

I'm checking whether the horn base at the scaled world coordinates clears the blade's height zone near the same x-position, confirming there's no overlap with the blade tip.

Now I'm sketching the gold ring details along each horn at three points with slightly increasing radius, then planning the cheek fan spikes as a trio on each side angled outward from the hinge area with varying lengths.

For the forehead gem, I'm placing a glowing teal octahedron into a gold cylindrical setting mounted on the cranium surface, oriented along the normal, and then laying out a row of spike cones along the skull crest at increasing elevation angles.

Now I'm sweeping a rod to form the neck connecting collar to cranium with a flattened bone-colored radius, then turning to the eyes — deciding to skip decal veins and instead give the eyes a glowing slit-pupil look using a textured plane with a teal ellipse and dark slit, angled outward on the face.

Working out that the eye plane needs to sit close to the spherical socket but small enough that its edges stay hidden behind the socket's curvature, so I'm sizing it down to roughly 0.04 wide to avoid clipping through the surface.

For a cleaner result, I decide to use a decal projected directly onto the socket sphere instead, since that conforms to the curvature naturally and still supports glow since decals return a textured Part. I'll sketch the eye texture as a 100x70 slit shape, then move on to planning the other textures needed: ghost, flame, runes, ribbon, lantern, and an emblem — likely a dragon-eye sigil placed on the gold root plate near the blade.

I'm sizing the emblem as a small circular gold-teal medallion placed on both front and back plate surfaces, giving me seven total textures to manage. Then I start roughing out part counts — vertebrae, barbs, teeth, chain links, lantern pieces, cloth, and rings — aiming for a total somewhere around 230 parts while keeping triangle counts reasonable, and I'm working out how the vertebrae's transverse spikes and neural spine fins should alternate along the shaft.

Writing lathe profile math...

I'll extend the core from y 0.2 to 1.82 for hooking, and add a ribbon ring collar at 1.76. I'm skipping the mid-shaft dragon-rib claws for now and will move on to the blade ribs and soul-flame details on the spine.

For joints, I'm settling on five: snath (root), head, jaw, blade, and lantern (child of snath, with chain attached). I'm assigning bones explicitly—shaft elements to snath, skull parts to head, jaw pieces to jaw, the blade to its own bone, lantern and chain together, and the counter horn back to snath.

Working through the API signatures now, assuming `part` takes geometry, color, and options like bone/at/dir/scale, while `spike` takes base point, direction, length, radius, and color options...

Still checking sweep, rod, extrude, lathe, and loft signatures...

input.command: cd src; grep -n "loft" builder.ts | head; grep -n "export type LoftStation" -A12 *.ts | head -40; grep -n "type SweepOptions" -A50 sweep.ts | head -90
cd samples; sed -n 1,60p frostAxe.ts; grep -n "glow(" soulScythe.ts | head -3; wc -l soulScythe.ts
